questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a building permits
questions.learningObjective: Explain what it means for a building to permit a play
questions.stem: In a planning memo on the proposed civic theatre, the architect argues that a building does more than hold a play; it permits certain kinds of play. Which claim best expresses that idea?

options.text: A building permits a play when it contains enough seats to hold large audiences
options.misconception: reduces permission to audience size

options.text: A building permits a play when its materials are fireproof and meet safety codes
options.misconception: treats safety compliance as artistic permission

options.text: A building permits a play by fixing what can be seen, heard and moved within it
A building permits a play when its architect has a personal taste in period rooms
options.misconception: grounds permission in the architect's preference

questions.explanation: A building's permitted plays are the ones its conditions allow: what the audience can see, where sound travels, how people move. Architecture narrows a director's choices before a word is spoken.
questions.hint: Ask what the building makes possible.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A thrust stage and its intimacy
questions.learningObjective: Infer what a short audience distance signals about a thrust

stimulus.body: The memo reports that the new studio theatre will have seating in raked rows on three sides, so that the audience sits close to the acting area on three sides and the fourth is left open. The architect notes that no seat is more than nine metres from the nearest performer.

questions.stem: In the memo describing the three-sided studio theatre, the nine-metre limit suggests what about the thrust configuration?

options.text: That performers can be seen from every seat, so the stage can be surrounded completely
options.misconception: assumes complete surround is the design

options.text: That the acoustics will be good, since close seating controls reflections
options.misconception: treats distance as an acoustic fix

options.text: That lighting can be simple, because close seating needs few fixtures
options.misconception: links seating distance to lighting complexity

options.text: That performers and audience share a room, which is the intimacy the thrust is chosen for

questions.explanation: A thrust stage pushes the audience around the playing area on three sides, so the playing space is surrounded rather than framed. The short distance to the nearest performer is what makes that closeness felt.
questions.hint: Think about where the audience sits.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A proscenium and the picture it enforces
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a proscenium frame enforces
questions.stem: Between site visits, the planner's memo on the new opera house records that the audience will look at the stage through a single framed opening. Which claim about that frame is best supported?

options.text: The frame fixes the picture the audience sees, so offstage action can be withheld from view
The frame adds nothing, since the audience always watches whatever the actors do
options.misconception: denies that framing affects what is seen

options.text: The frame enlarges the stage, since the opening shows more of the stage floor
options.misconception: claims the frame increases the visible area

options.text: The frame makes the theatre cheaper to build, because one opening is simpler than several
options.misconception: explains the frame by construction cost

questions.explanation: A proscenium arch defines a single rectangular picture and hides whatever lies outside it. That enforced picture is why the play must reveal its secrets by opening the frame or using the space behind it.
questions.hint: Ask what falls outside the frame.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: An open stage and its sightlines
questions.learningObjective: Explain how sightlines constrain what may be staged
questions.stem: In the memo on the market-square performance site, the planner asks how sightlines shape what a director can stage. Write the explanation she needs.

answer.exemplar: Sightlines determine what the audience is able to see from where it sits. On an open stage every viewer has a different angle, so a director must stage an action that reads from several directions at once, or accept that some spectators lose the scene. A building that fixes the viewing position removes that problem, and with it removes a set of practical difficulties that open staging has to solve.

questions.explanation: The answer must explain how varying audience angles constrain what can be staged and how a fixed viewpoint changes the difficulty. The exemplar links sightlines to staging practice.
questions.hint: Ask what changes when angles vary.

questions.stem: At the budget meeting for the touring theatre, the planner argues that a touring company's building is barely its own. Which argument supports her?

options.text: Because the company must apply for every venue's licence before it can perform there
options.misconception: grounds the claim in licensing paperwork

options.text: Because the company has to work inside whatever building it is given, with little control over its shape
Because touring companies pay more per seat than companies with their own theatres
options.misconception: explains the constraint in financial terms

options.text: Because the audience travels to the company, so the building matters less than the road
options.misconception: moves attention away from the building

questions.explanation: A touring company brings its production to buildings it did not choose, so it must adapt staging, scenery and acoustics to each one. The building constrains the company far more than it constrains a resident company.
questions.hint: Ask who chose the room.

questions.learningObjective: Synthesise what follows from a repertory company staying in one building
questions.stem: In the memo on the new rehearsal centre, the planner claims that a repertory company depends on a building that stays the same. Which set of claims follows?

options.text: It can hire different designers each season, since a fixed building never shapes a design
options.misconception: denies that the building shapes design

options.text: It must rebuild its scenery each year, since resident companies never reuse a set
options.misconception: claims resident companies never reuse sets

options.text: It cannot tour, because a repertory company by definition stays in one place
options.misconception: defines repertory as permanent residence

options.text: It can plan a season of sets for one space, so the building becomes part of the design

questions.explanation: A repertory company returns to the same building, so it can design for known conditions and reuse what it has built. The building therefore stops being neutral and becomes a fixed term in the company's planning.
questions.hint: Ask what comes back every season.

questions.topic: A licensing system and what it censors
questions.learningObjective: Describe what a licence does to a text
questions.stem: During the consultation on the new theatre, the planner's memo records the licensing officer's remark about what the censor examines. Which reading best fits the function of a licence?

options.text: A licence checks that the text is financially safe, so companies avoid losses
options.misconception: treats licensing as financial protection

options.text: A licence confirms the play is famous, so only well-known works may be performed
options.misconception: makes licensing a test of reputation

options.text: A licence checks the text against rules about what may be shown, which may cut or forbid it
A licence awards a monopoly on the work, so only one company may stage it
options.misconception: confuses licensing with exclusive rights

questions.explanation: A licence is granted after a text is examined against rules about what may be shown publicly. The examiner can require cuts, restrict the performance or refuse it, so the licence directly limits what an audience may see.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a building permits
questions.learningObjective: Infer what an acoustic treatment permits

stimulus.body: The memo notes that the concert hall's reverberation time is 2.1 seconds, so a whisper at the front of the stage is still audible at the back. The architect proposes leaving the room acoustically dead so that text can be heard clearly.

questions.stem: In the memo about the concert hall's reverberation, the proposed dead acoustic is intended to do what?

options.text: Make the hall usable for spoken drama, since speech will carry without amplification
options.misconception: assumes speech needs no help in a large hall

options.text: Give the text priority over music, since a short reverberation protects the clarity of words
Reduce the building's cost, since acoustic treatment is expensive to specify
options.misconception: explains the treatment by cost

options.text: Preserve the hall's original sound, since its concrete shell gives it a characteristic tone
options.misconception: treats the treatment as preserving a tone

questions.explanation: Reverberation smears sound and blurs the edges of speech. Shortening it prioritises the clarity of words over the resonance of music, which is what makes the room permit spoken text.
questions.hint: Ask what the room must not blur.

questions.topic: A thrust stage and its intimacy
questions.learningObjective: Identify the chief benefit of a thrust stage
questions.stem: Between council deputations, the planner argues that the thrust stage at the old brewery is the building's chief asset. Which benefit does a thrust chiefly offer?

options.text: It seats more people than a proscenium of the same size, because the space is used on three sides
options.misconception: credits the thrust with extra capacity

options.text: It lets the audience sit close to the performers on three sides, which shortens the distance between them
It removes the need for a lighting rig, because no one looks at the ceiling
options.misconception: claims the thrust removes lighting needs

options.text: It guarantees good acoustics, because sound spreads evenly around a thrust
options.misconception: assumes thrust plans solve acoustics

questions.explanation: The thrust's defining feature is audience seating on three sides of the playing area. That geometry brings spectators close to the action on three quarters of the perimeter, which is where its intimacy comes from.
questions.hint: Count the sides with seats.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A proscenium and the picture it enforces
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a proscenium enforces and how directors work with it
questions.stem: In the memo about the auditorium renovation, the planner must explain what a proscenium enforces and why directors work with it. Write her explanation.

answer.exemplar: A proscenium arch enforces a single framed picture, so the audience looks at the stage from one direction and cannot see around the edge of the set. That constraint is not a pure obstacle: it lets the designers and actors control what is visible and when. Working with the frame means revealing the picture deliberately, and the moment a set opens or a curtain moves becomes meaningful because the frame had kept it hidden.

questions.explanation: The answer must define the enforced picture and then turn it into a working constraint rather than a bare limitation. The exemplar shows how the frame makes revelation meaningful.
questions.hint: Say what the frame allows control over.

questions.learningObjective: Defend open staging against the claim that it fails
questions.stem: At the site inspection of the plaza, the planner defends open staging against the claim that it always goes wrong. Which argument is strongest?

options.text: Open staging always goes wrong because no designer can light an area with many angles
options.misconception: attacks open staging purely on lighting

options.text: Open staging always goes wrong because audiences cannot agree on where to look
options.misconception: assumes audiences cannot share a focus

options.text: Open staging always goes wrong because directors lose control of the crowd's attention
options.misconception: treats the problem as control of attention

options.text: Open staging works when the action is placed for many angles, so the failure lies in the design

questions.explanation: The strongest defence accepts that multiple sightlines are hard and locates the failure in the design rather than in the format. An action staged for one angle will always break for another, so the discipline is what makes the form work.
questions.hint: Ask where the fault lies.

options.misconception: puts casting in the wrong place

questions.learningObjective: Identify what a permanent base gives a resident company
questions.stem: During the lease negotiation for the new home of the resident company, the planner weighs what the company gains from one permanent base. Which gain matters most?

options.text: A known space that lets the company design for particular sightlines and acoustics over time
A cheaper building, because a resident company qualifies for the city's rate relief
options.misconception: grounds the gain in a rate saving

options.text: A larger stage, since permanent tenants always receive the bigger halls
options.misconception: assumes tenancy brings a larger stage

options.text: A broader audience, because residents attract more ticket buyers than visitors do
options.misconception: credits residency with wider appeal

questions.explanation: The point of a permanent base is not size or subsidy but knowledge of the room. A company that returns to the same building can plan for its exact geometry, so design improves across seasons.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A licensing system and what it censors
questions.learningObjective: Describe the combined powers a licence can exercise

stimulus.body: The memo attaches the examiner's report for a play about drug misuse. The report rules that two references must be removed and that the performance may not be given to audiences under sixteen, while leaving the central scene otherwise unchanged.

questions.stem: In the memo attaching the examiner's report, the combination of cuts and an age restriction shows what a licence can do?

options.text: It can alter the text and still limit who may see it, so censorship works on content and on audience
It can only stop a production outright, since any alteration would change the author's work
options.misconception: treats censorship as all-or-nothing

options.text: It can only restrict who may attend, since the text itself is considered untouchable
options.misconception: makes the text untouchable

options.text: It can only require cuts, since age limits are set by the theatre rather than the licence
options.misconception: credits age limits to the theatre

questions.explanation: The examiner's report shows both powers exercised in one decision: two references removed from the text and the audience narrowed. Censorship therefore acts on what is said and on who stands in the room to hear it.
questions.hint: Note what was removed and who was excluded.

questions.topic: What a building permits
questions.learningObjective: Explain how fixed dimensions decide which plays fit
questions.stem: In the memo assessing the disused cinema conversion, the planner argues that the building's existing dimensions decide which plays can be staged there. Which claim is best supported?

options.text: The building permits the plays whose sets and crowds fit inside those fixed dimensions
The building permits the plays whose themes suit its location on the high street
options.misconception: reads permission from location and taste

options.text: The building permits the plays that it can afford to heat and light at full capacity

options.misconception: attributes permission to the owners' taste

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A thrust stage and its intimacy
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a thrust stage is chosen for intimacy
questions.stem: At the design review of the studio theatre, the planner writes out why a thrust stage is chosen for intimacy. Write her explanation.

answer.exemplar: A thrust stage is chosen for intimacy because it places spectators on three sides of the playing area instead of facing it from one side. There is no fourth wall to hide behind, so an actor cannot point at a wall and claim no one is there; the audience is present from several angles at once. Distance also shrinks, and a small audience sees detail that a large house would lose.

questions.explanation: The answer must connect the three-sided seating to closeness and to the loss of a separate address, which is what produces intimacy. The exemplar does both.
questions.hint: Say what the fourth wall would allow.

questions.stem: During the committee meeting on the opera house, the planner argues that a proscenium is a way of seeing rather than a mere shape of wall. Which argument is strongest?

options.text: Because the frame was invented by printers and copied into theatres for convenience
options.misconception: explains the form by its history of copying

options.text: Because it fixes one picture for the audience, and every staging choice must answer to that picture
Because it costs more to build than an open stage in the same hall
options.misconception: grounds the claim in construction cost

options.text: Because it was required by the licensing rules of the period
options.misconception: claims rules forced the form

questions.explanation: The frame is a way of seeing because it determines the audience's single point of view and makes every visual decision answerable to it. Its effects on the play are therefore structural, not decorative.
questions.hint: Ask what the frame decides.

questions.stem: In the memo on the disused chapel conversion, the planner needs to write what a building permits. Write her explanation.

answer.exemplar: A building permits certain plays because it fixes conditions the playwright and director cannot change: the size and shape of the room, the height above the stage, the number of doors, the distance between the audience and the actors, and the noise the walls will carry. questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE

questions.learningObjective: Explain what a licensing system censors and why it matters
questions.stem: At the licensing committee's hearing, the planner must write what a licensing system censors and why it matters. Write her note.

answer.exemplar: A licensing system censors what an audience may be shown and heard: the words of the text, the images on the stage and the age of those allowed to attend. It matters because the examination happens before any performance, so the version the audience finally sees is already the version the examiner allowed. Censorship therefore operates most often as an edit rather than a prohibition, quietly changing plays while leaving their names on the poster.

options.misconception: invents a funding dependency

questions.explanation: The production must be settled before the tour starts, because the conditions it meets cannot be known in advance. The halls are the part the company accepts, and flexibility must be built into the work in advance.
questions.hint: Ask what must be settled first.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A repertory company and its ensemble
questions.learningObjective: Identify what keeps a repertory ensemble stable
questions.stem: During the residency review, the planner asks what keeps a repertory ensemble stable. Which answer is sound?

options.text: Keeping the building busy all year, since constant work holds a company together
options.misconception: credits activity with holding the company

options.text: Keeping the same members across seasons, since continuity is what the ensemble is made of
Keeping the repertoire varied, since a company needs new challenges each term
options.misconception: makes variety the source of stability

options.text: Keeping the audiences growing, since a company with no audience cannot keep its players
options.misconception: grounds stability in audience size

questions.explanation: An ensemble is a set of relationships built over time, and those relationships are what allow trust between roles and cover at short notice. Keeping the members is therefore the condition of the stability, not the box office.
questions.hint: Ask what is carried between seasons.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A licensing system and what it censors
questions.learningObjective: Infer what a rewriting procedure shows about censorship

stimulus.body: The memo recounts that the examiner's office read the script, then told the company that a scene set in a brothel could not be staged as written. The company rewrote the scene, and the licence was issued for the rewritten version without further comment.

questions.stem: In the memo recounting the rewritten scene, the examiner's procedure shows what about censorship?

options.text: That censorship refuses texts outright, since the rewrite proves the work was banned
options.misconception: reads the rewrite as a ban

options.text: That censorship depends on public complaint, since the memo implies one was made
options.misconception: invents a complaint as the trigger

options.text: That censorship can work as an edit, reshaping a text rather than removing it
That censorship falls to individual local officials, since the examiner's office is small
options.misconception: makes the decision about office size

questions.explanation: The company was not refused; it was told to change the scene and was then licensed. That sequence shows censorship operating most often as an edit, altering the text while leaving the work in circulation.
questions.hint: Note what the company did next.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a building permits
questions.learningObjective: Explain why one play differs across two buildings
questions.stem: On the inspection of the new studio, the planner explains why two buildings can host the same play differently. Which claim is sound?

options.text: Because each building fixes its own conditions, so the same text meets different limits in each
Because the better building draws better performances, since quality of staff decides all
options.misconception: blames the building's staffing

options.text: Because audiences vary, so the same play suits different towns in different ways
options.misconception: grounds the difference in local audience taste

options.text: Because the weather changes how plays are received, so a wet month alters a text
options.misconception: makes weather determine the reception

questions.explanation: A play meets the fixed conditions of whichever building hosts it: scale, sound, access and view. The same text therefore meets different limits in each room, and the staging adapts to what the room offers.
questions.hint: Ask what each room supplies.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A thrust stage and its intimacy
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a thrust stage offers a company
questions.stem: In the memo on the brewery conversion, the planner writes what a thrust stage offers a company. Write her note.

answer.exemplar: A thrust offers a company a playing space that is surrounded rather than faced. Audiences on three sides cannot all be given a separate wall to perform against, so the staging has to work with the room's openness, which pushes the company towards movement, levels and continual reorganisation of the space. It also keeps the audience close, so small actions register.

questions.explanation: The note must describe the three-sided arrangement and connect it to both intimacy and the demands it makes on staging. The exemplar covers both.
questions.hint: Say what the missing wall forces.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A proscenium and the picture it enforces
questions.learningObjective: Dispute the claim that a proscenium is a frame for decoration
questions.stem: In the committee discussion of the opera house, the planner disputes the claim that a proscenium is a frame for decoration. Which argument is best?

options.text: Because the frame fixes what the audience may see, so the play's effects depend on it rather than on costume
Because the frame was standard for centuries, so old buildings had to follow the standard
options.misconception: grounds the argument in historical habit

options.text: Because the frame is cheaper than a thrust, so theatres chose it for reasons of money
options.misconception: makes the frame a matter of economy

options.text: Because the frame is the only shape that can hold modern lighting equipment
options.misconception: claims the frame suits modern lighting

questions.explanation: The argument locates the frame's importance in what it determines rather than in what it displays. Because it fixes the visible picture, every visual effect is delivered through it, making it a structural condition.
questions.hint: Ask what the frame decides for the play.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: An open stage and its sightlines
questions.learningObjective: Identify what an open stage asks of a designer
questions.stem: In the final memo before the plaza season opens, the planner records what the open stage asks of a designer. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: The design must work from several directions, since every spectator sees a different part of the action
options.misconception: credits the design with serving only the best seat

options.text: The design must be simple, since complex scenery cannot be read from a distance
options.misconception: reduces the demand to plainness

options.text: The design must be legible from more than one angle, so that most of the crowd can follow it
The design must be scaled up, since distant spectators cannot see small actions in an open space
options.misconception: assumes open spaces need larger scale

questions.explanation: With viewers around the playing area, no single composition serves everyone, so the design has to be readable from several directions at once. That is a demand on legibility rather than on scale or simplicity.
questions.hint: Ask what most of the crowd can follow.
